  SELECT COALESCE(k.workspace_id, 'default') AS workspace_id, u.model,
         u.input_tokens AS inp, u.cache_creation_5m_tokens AS w5, u.cache_creation_1h_tokens AS w1,
         u.cache_read_input_tokens AS rd, u.output_tokens AS outp
  FROM messages_usage u
  JOIN api_keys k ON k.api_key_id = u.api_key_id
  WHERE u.created_at >= DATE '{{day}}'
    AND u.created_at <  DATE '{{day}}' + 1
), g AS (
  SELECT workspace_id, model, COUNT(*) AS requests,
         SUM(inp) AS inp, SUM(w5) AS w5, SUM(w1) AS w1, SUM(rd) AS rd, SUM(outp) AS outp
  FROM day_usage
  GROUP BY workspace_id, model
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_requests}}
), costed AS (
  SELECT g.*, g.inp + g.w5 + g.w1 + g.rd AS prompt_tokens,
         (g.inp * p.input_usd_per_mtok
          + g.w5 * p.input_usd_per_mtok * 1.25
          + g.w1 * p.input_usd_per_mtok * 2
          + g.rd * p.input_usd_per_mtok * 0.1
          + g.outp * p.output_usd_per_mtok) / 1000000 AS actual,
         ((g.inp + g.w5 + g.w1 + g.rd) * p.input_usd_per_mtok
          + g.outp * p.output_usd_per_mtok) / 1000000 AS uncached
  FROM g JOIN model_prices p ON p.model = g.model
)

       ROUND(rd::numeric / prompt_tokens, 4) AS cache_read_share,
       ROUND(actual, 4)            AS actual_cost_usd,
       ROUND(uncached, 4)          AS uncached_cost_usd,
       ROUND(uncached - actual, 4) AS net_savings_usd
FROM costed

WITH deltas AS (
  SELECT e.request_id, e.seq, e.event_ts,
         e.event_ts - LAG(e.event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY e.request_id ORDER BY e.seq) AS gap
  FROM stream_events e
  WHERE e.event_type = 'content_block_delta'
), per_request AS (
  SELECT q.request_id, q.model, q.started_at,
         (SELECT MIN(d.event_ts) FROM deltas d WHERE d.request_id = q.request_id) AS first_delta_ts,
         (SELECT MAX(d.gap) FROM deltas d WHERE d.request_id = q.request_id) AS max_gap,
         (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM deltas d WHERE d.request_id = q.request_id) AS deltas,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM stream_events s WHERE s.request_id = q.request_id AND s.event_type = 'message_stop') AS stopped,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM stream_events s WHERE s.request_id = q.request_id AND s.event_type = 'error') AS errored
  FROM stream_requests q
), measured AS (
  SELECT request_id, model,
         (EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM first_delta_ts - started_at) * 1000)::bigint AS ttft_ms,
         (EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM max_gap) * 1000)::bigint AS max_gap_ms,
         deltas,
         CASE WHEN stopped THEN 'completed' WHEN errored THEN 'error' ELSE 'truncated' END AS outcome
  FROM per_request
)
SELECT request_id, model, ttft_ms, max_gap_ms, deltas, outcome
FROM measured
WHERE outcome <> 'completed' OR ttft_ms > {{ttft_ms}} OR max_gap_ms > {{gap_ms}}
ORDER BY request_id;

Explanation. The deltas CTE filters to content_block_delta before the window function, so LAG compares each piece of text with the previous piece of text; pings, block starts and message events can never split a silence. MAX(gap) ignores the NULL of the first delta, so one delta gives NULL. TTFT is the first delta's time minus started_at. The per-request values are taken from stream_requests outward (correlated subqueries here; a LEFT JOIN to a grouped CTE is equivalent), so requests with no deltas, or no events at all, stay in. The outcome is a three-way CASE in priority order. The WHERE clause is NULL-aware by construction: a NULL TTFT or gap makes its comparison NULL, which is not true, so only the outcome can flag such a request. Milliseconds come from EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM interval) * 1000, exact in numeric in PostgreSQL 14 and later, then cast to bigint.

Complexity. One sort of the deltas by (request_id, seq) for the window (the primary key provides it), then per-request aggregates: O(n log n), or O(n) with the index order. A production version groups once per request instead of four correlated lookups.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake: TIMESTAMPDIFF(millisecond, a, b), BOOLOR_AGG for the outcome flags, QUALIFY if you take the first delta by seq with a window. BigQuery: TIMESTAMP_DIFF(b, a, MILLISECOND); LOGICAL_OR. Spark SQL: unix_millis(b) - unix_millis(a); windowed lag works the same; no FILTER, use max(case …). MySQL 8: TIMESTAMPDIFF(MICROSECOND, a, b) DIV 1000, and LAG over a derived table of deltas.

Edge cases built into the data. Pings inside every stall and before the first delta (every level); a slow first token; a stall over the gap threshold; events sharing a millisecond, values exactly at each threshold, and streams ended by an error event (Hard and Very Hard); an error before any delta, a stream that stops with neither message_stop nor error, a completed single-delta stream that must not be flagged, a slow single-delta stream, a request with no events, and events stored out of order (Very Hard).

Common mistakes. LAG over all events and filtering afterwards (pings hide the stall); measuring TTFT from message_start; ordering by event_ts without seq (harmless for gaps, but a smell); >=; treating a NULL gap as 0 or as a problem; inner joins that lose requests without events; labelling every unfinished stream 'error'; returning seconds or an interval instead of integer milliseconds.

(1) Per open request keep started_at, last delta time, max gap, count and flags; emit when message_stop or error arrives, or when a request has been silent past a hard timeout (then it is truncated). (2) Percentiles are not additive; keep a mergeable histogram or sketch (fixed buckets, t-digest, DDSketch) per model and hour and merge for longer ranges. (3) Compare gaps with output position and output length per model; network problems correlate with client region or connection and appear across models, generation effects with long outputs on one model. WITH attempts AS (
  SELECT b.job_id, q.custom_id, b.batch_id, b.created_at, b.processing_status,
         r.result_type, r.output_tokens,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY b.job_id, q.custom_id
                            ORDER BY b.created_at DESC, b.batch_id DESC) AS recency
  FROM batch_requests q
  JOIN batches b ON b.batch_id = q.batch_id
  LEFT JOIN batch_results r ON r.batch_id = q.batch_id AND r.custom_id = q.custom_id
), items AS (
  SELECT job_id, custom_id,
         COALESCE(BOOL_OR(result_type = 'succeeded'), false)                  AS ever_succeeded,
         MAX(processing_status) FILTER (WHERE recency = 1)                     AS latest_status,
         BOOL_OR(result_type IS NOT NULL) FILTER (WHERE recency = 1)           AS latest_has_result
  FROM attempts
  GROUP BY job_id, custom_id
), successes AS (
  SELECT job_id, custom_id, output_tokens,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY job_id, custom_id ORDER BY created_at, batch_id) AS nth
  FROM attempts
  WHERE result_type = 'succeeded'
), dup AS (
  SELECT job_id, custom_id, COUNT(*) AS wins,
         COALESCE(SUM(output_tokens) FILTER (WHERE nth > 1), 0) AS wasted
  FROM successes
  GROUP BY job_id, custom_id
)
SELECT i.job_id,
       COUNT(*)                                                                         AS items,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE i.ever_succeeded)                                         AS succeeded,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT i.ever_succeeded AND i.latest_status = 'ended' AND i.latest_has_result)     AS retry,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT i.ever_succeeded AND i.latest_status = 'ended' AND NOT i.latest_has_result) AS missing,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT i.ever_succeeded AND i.latest_status <> 'ended')     AS in_flight,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE d.wins > 1)                                               AS duplicate_successes,
       COALESCE(SUM(d.wasted), 0)                                                       AS wasted_output_tokens
FROM items i
LEFT JOIN dup d ON d.job_id = i.job_id AND d.custom_id = i.custom_id
GROUP BY i.job_id
ORDER BY i.job_id;

Explanation. One row per attempt: every batch_requests row with its batch and, through a LEFT JOIN, its result if one exists. recency = 1 marks an item's latest attempt (by created_at DESC, batch_id DESC, so ties are deterministic). Reducing to one row per item gives ever_succeeded (any success at all, so a success followed by a failed resubmission is still succeeded), the latest attempt's batch status and whether it has a result. Those three facts classify each item into exactly one bucket. Successes are numbered by the same ascending order; every success after the first is wasted. Items join their duplicate summary with a LEFT JOIN so items with no duplicates stay.

Complexity. A sort of attempts by (job_id, custom_id, created_at, batch_id) for the windows, a hash join to results on (batch_id, custom_id) and two aggregations: O(n log n) in attempts. Incrementally, only items with an attempt in a newly ended batch change.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). Snowflake and BigQuery: QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…) = 1 for the latest attempt; BOOLOR_AGG / LOGICAL_OR for BOOL_OR; COUNT_IF / COUNTIF for COUNT(*) FILTER. Spark SQL: bool_or exists, count_if replaces FILTER. MySQL 8: no BOOL_OR or FILTER; use MAX(result_type = 'succeeded') and SUM(CASE …).

Edge cases built into the data. Items failed and retried, and one failed item not yet resubmitted (every level); an item resubmitted after it had succeeded, and two batches created in the same second that both succeed for the same item, so batch_id decides which success is first and which tokens are wasted (Hard and Very Hard); an item that succeeded and then failed on a resubmission, an ended batch with no result for its item, and a batch still in progress (Very Hard).

Counting request rows as items; classifying by the latest attempt only; an inner join to results (missing items vanish and items shrinks); treating in-progress items as missing; wasting the first success too; ordering successes by created_at alone; grouping items by custom_id across jobs.

(2) Resubmit only items whose state is not succeeded, from that state table, and record the resubmission before submitting; keep custom_id stable per item so results map back. (3) Compare the batch's own result counts (the API reports counts per result type when a batch ends) with rows exported per batch; alert when an ended batch's exported results do not equal its request count. def tool_call_stats(events, timeout_ms):
    calls = {}        # (conversation_id, tool_use_id) -> [tool, start_ts, resolved]
    per_tool = {}
    unmatched = 0
    spans = []        # (start, end) of every call, half-open
    for ts, conv, kind, tool_use_id, tool, is_error in events:
        key = (conv, tool_use_id)
        call = calls.get(key)
        if kind == 'use':
            if call is None:                      # a re-delivered use is ignored
                calls[key] = [tool, ts, False]
                per_tool.setdefault(tool, [0, 0, 0, 0])[0] += 1
            continue
        if call is None:                          # no earlier use for this key
            unmatched += 1
            continue
        if call[2]:                               # the call already has its result
            continue
        call[2] = True
        stats = per_tool[call[0]]
        if ts - call[1] > timeout_ms:             # it had already timed out
            stats[3] += 1
            spans.append((call[1], call[1] + timeout_ms))
        else:
            stats[2 if is_error else 1] += 1
            spans.append((call[1], ts))
    for tool, start, resolved in calls.values():
        if not resolved:                          # never answered
            per_tool[tool][3] += 1
            spans.append((start, start + timeout_ms))
    points = []
    for start, end in spans:
        if end > start:
            points.append((start, 1))
            points.append((end, -1))
    points.sort()                                 # at equal times, -1 sorts before +1
    peak = cur = 0
    for _, d in points:
        cur += d
        if cur > peak:
            peak = cur
    return per_tool, unmatched, peak

Explanation. One pass over the events with a dict keyed by (conversation_id, tool_use_id): a use creates the call if the key is new (a re-delivered use is ignored); a result for an unknown key is unmatched; the first result for a known call resolves it (late ones become timeouts with an interval capped at the deadline) and later results are ignored. Calls that never resolve time out. The peak is a sweep over interval endpoints: (t, +1) and (t, −1); Python sorts tuples so −1 comes before +1 at the same time, which is exactly the half-open rule. Empty intervals are skipped.

Complexity. O(n) for the pass and O(c log c) for sorting 2c endpoints, c ≤ n calls; O(n) memory. The naive versions are quadratic: scanning back through the log for each result's use, or counting overlaps for every pair of calls. With 200 000 events and hundreds of calls in flight both take far longer than the limit; the reference takes well under a second.

Common mistakes. >= for the timeout; counting a late result as unmatched or as ok; counting a second use as a new call; keying by tool_use_id alone (Very Hard has the same id in two conversations); sorting endpoints with +1 first (adjacent calls overlap and the peak is one too high); forgetting calls without results in the sweep; counting a result that precedes its use as matched.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Keep open calls in a min-heap by deadline; at each event pop calls whose deadline has passed (they end at their deadline) and maintain the in-flight count; a result decrements immediately. A late result finds its call already expired and is ignored. (2) Keep one counter per tool and one overall in the same sweep; the overall peak is not the sum of per-tool peaks. (3) Durations near the timeout and zero-length calls change; key the order by one collector's clock or apply measured offsets, and treat results within the skew of the deadline as uncertain. (4) Results for unknown ids come from a use lost in transit, ids rewritten by a client, results sent to the wrong conversation, or clock skew putting a result before its use; join by id across conversations and by time to see which.

Rubric anchors. 2: correct counts but a quadratic peak or matching, or a boundary error. 3: correct and O(n log n). 4: also a streaming design with a deadline heap and an honest treatment of skew.

import heapq


def run_jobs(jobs, slots, cancels):
    cancel_at = dict(cancels)
    out = {jid: [0, 0, 0, None] for jid, *_ in jobs}       # done, canceled, expired, last finish
    by_model = {}
    for idx, (jid, model, sub, dl, durs) in enumerate(jobs):
        by_model.setdefault(model, []).append((sub, idx, jid, dl, durs))
    for model, js in by_model.items():                     # models never share slots
        js.sort()
        cl = sorted((cancel_at[j[2]], j[2]) for j in js if j[2] in cancel_at)
        info = {jid: (dl, durs) for _, _, jid, dl, durs in js}
        pos = {jid: 0 for jid in info}
        free, running, ready = slots[model], [], []
        i = ci = 0
        while i < len(js) or running or ci < len(cl):
            t = min(x for x in (js[i][0] if i < len(js) else None,
                                running[0] if running else None,
                                cl[ci][0] if ci < len(cl) else None) if x is not None)
            while running and running[0] == t:             # 1. finished requests free slots
                heapq.heappop(running)
                free += 1
            while i < len(js) and js[i][0] == t:           # 2. submissions join the queue
                sub, idx, jid, dl, durs = js[i]
                heapq.heappush(ready, (dl, sub, idx, jid))
                i += 1
            while ci < len(cl) and cl[ci][0] == t:         # 3. cancels before any start at t
                c, jid = cl[ci]
                ci += 1
                dl, durs = info[jid]
                if c < dl and pos[jid] < len(durs):
                    out[jid][1] += len(durs) - pos[jid]
                    pos[jid] = len(durs)
            while free and ready:                          # 4. earliest deadline first
                dl, sub, idx, jid = ready[0]
                durs = info[jid][1]
                p = pos[jid]
                if p == len(durs):
                    heapq.heappop(ready)
                    continue
                if t >= dl:                                # too late to start: the rest expires
                    heapq.heappop(ready)
                    out[jid][2] += len(durs) - p
                    pos[jid] = len(durs)
                    continue
                end = t + durs[p]
                heapq.heappush(running, end)
                free -= 1
                pos[jid] = p + 1
                rec = out[jid]
                rec[0] += 1
                rec[3] = end if rec[3] is None or end > rec[3] else rec[3]
        for jid, (dl, durs) in info.items():               # whatever never started expired
            if pos[jid] < len(durs):

Explanation. A discrete-event simulation per model (models share nothing). The only moments that change state are submissions, finishes and cancels, so the loop jumps to the smallest of the next submission, the earliest running finish and the next cancel. Within one second the specification's order is applied literally: free slots, enqueue submissions, apply cancels, then fill slots. Running requests sit in a min-heap of finish times; waiting jobs sit in a min-heap keyed by (deadline, submit, position), which is exactly the tie-break. A job stays at the top while it has requests to start, so consecutive slots go to the same job until it is exhausted. Deadlines need no events of their own: a job whose deadline has passed is expired lazily when it reaches the top with a free slot, and any job left with unstarted requests at the end has expired. Lazy expiry gives the same counts because a request can only start at an event time, and the check t < deadline is made at the moment of starting. Cancels after the deadline are ignored, so expired requests are never relabelled as canceled.

Complexity. O((R + J) log J + R log S) time for R requests, J jobs and S slots, O(R + J) memory. The timing test (8 000 jobs, about 205 000 requests, all submitted within 2 000 seconds) runs in about 0.2–0.3 s in CPython. The same loop with the waiting jobs kept in a plain list and scanned with min() at every start took about 12 s; simulating second by second is worse still, because deadlines are up to 90 000 seconds away.

In a SQL engine this kind of stateful scheduling does not express well (it is inherently sequential); a Spark version would group by model and run the simulation per group with mapGroups/applyInPandas. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A slot freed at t reused at t; a later submission with an earlier deadline served first; a request started before the deadline that finishes after it, together with a request that cannot start exactly at its deadline; the same with the deadline one second later; equal deadlines broken by submission time and then input order; a deadline equal to the submission time; (Hard) models that do not share slots, a job with no requests ((0, 0, 0, None)), a busy model whose waiting job expires while another model is idle; (Very Hard) a cancel at the same second as a start, a cancel after the deadline, a cancel while every request is running, and a cancel that frees the queue for another job.

Common mistakes. FIFO by submission instead of earliest deadline; t <= deadline for starting; refusing to start a request that would finish after the deadline (the specification allows it); filling slots before freeing the ones that finish at the same second; counting requests that were running at cancel time as canceled; labelling requests canceled after the deadline; sharing one pool of slots across models; a global second-by-second loop; re-sorting the queue at every start.

EDF minimises the maximum lateness on one machine and is optimal for feasibility of preemptive single-machine schedules, but with non-preemptive requests and several slots it is a heuristic: a long request started for an early-deadline job can block several short jobs that would otherwise all have met their deadlines. def plan_evals(suites, budget, required):
    parent = {sid: p for sid, p, _, _ in suites}
    kids = {sid: [] for sid in parent}
    kids[None] = []
    for sid, p, _, _ in suites:
        kids[p].append(sid)
    cost = {sid: c for sid, _, c, _ in suites}
    value = {sid: v for sid, _, _, v in suites}
    cost[None] = value[None] = 0
    scale = sum(cost.values()) + 1               # score = coverage * scale - hours
    must = {None}                                # required suites and all their ancestors
    for sid in required:
        while sid not in must:
            must.add(sid)
            sid = parent[sid]
    NEG = float("-inf")

    def take(g, sid):                            # g with sid run on top of it
        c, s = cost[sid], value[sid] * scale - cost[sid]
        if c > budget:
            return [NEG] * (budget + 1)
        return [NEG] * c + [x + s for x in g[: budget + 1 - c]]

    # g[b]: best score of the decisions made so far using at most b hours.
    # A frame is [suite, g before its subtree, g with it run, next child index].
    start = [0] * (budget + 1)
    stack = [[None, start, take(start, None), 0]]
    while True:
        frame = stack[-1]
        sid, before, taken, i = frame
        if i < len(kids[sid]):
            frame[3] += 1
            child = kids[sid][i]
            stack.append([child, taken, take(taken, child), 0])
            continue
        result = taken if sid in must else list(map(max, before, taken))
        stack.pop()
        if not stack:
            break
        stack[-1][2] = result                    # the parent continues from here
    best = result[budget]
    if best == NEG:
        return None
    v = -(-best // scale)
    return (v, v * scale - best)

Explanation. This is a knapsack with precedence constraints that form a forest (a virtual root holds the base suites). The reference passes a budget array down the tree: g[b] is the best score of all decisions made before reaching a suite, using at most b hours. Taking the suite shifts the array by its hours and adds its score; its children then make their own decisions starting from that array; the suite's result is the element-wise maximum of "skipped" (the array it received) and "taken" (the array after its subtree), except that a suite that is required or has a required descendant cannot be skipped. Each suite costs O(budget) work, so the whole run is O(n · budget). The tie rule is folded into one integer: score = coverage × scale − hours with scale larger than any hour total, so a larger score means more coverage, then fewer hours. The traversal uses an explicit stack because families can be thousands of suites deep. An equivalent method lists suites in depth-first order and fills f[i][b] = max(take: f[i+1][b − h_i] + v_i, skip: f[i + size_i][b]) from the end.

Complexity. O(n · budget) time; O(budget · depth) memory for the stack of arrays (O(n · budget) for the depth-first-order table). The 3 000-suite, 2 000-hour timing test runs in well under a second in CPython. The classic child-merge tree knapsack is O(n · budget²) — about 10¹⁰ steps here; a naive version took about 40 seconds at only 200 suites. Subset enumeration is 2ⁿ.

In Java or C++ the same arrays are long[] and the "take" is a shifted loop; a recursion of depth 2 500 is usually fine in C++ but not on the default JVM thread stack for much deeper trees, and CPython's default limit is about 1 000. Scaling the tie-break into one integer needs 64-bit arithmetic in typed languages. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A high-coverage extension whose base is expensive (one hour short of affording both), the same with the budget exactly enough, equal coverage with different hours, an extension listed before its base, budget 0, nothing fits; (Hard) a required extension that forces its base even though that lowers coverage, required suites that do not fit (None), required suites that exactly fill the budget, an empty gate; (Very Hard) zero-hour suites under a zero-hour base, a required suite at the bottom of a 3 000-suite chain, and the same chain without the gate and one hour short.

Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Change detection. A change log from the document store (CDC or an event per write) produces (doc_id, content_hash, changed_at). A enrichment_state table keyed by (doc_id) holds the current content_hash and the (content_hash, prompt_version, model_snapshot) of the last valid enrichment. Work is due when the current tuple has no valid result. Hashing content (not updated_at) makes no-op saves free and catches edits within one second.
  • Work units and ids. A work unit is (doc_id, content_hash, prompt_version, model_snapshot). Its custom id is a deterministic short hash of that tuple (custom ids have length limits), with a work_unit table mapping id → tuple. Units are written with status queued before any submission, so a crash never loses track of what was sent.
  • Submission. A scheduler packs queued units into batches below the documented size limits, records batch_id against each unit (queued → submitted) in the same transaction that stores the provider's batch id, and submits under a per-pipeline token budget so the organization's shared limits keep headroom for interactive products. If the process crashes between the API call and the commit, the next run lists recent batches and reconciles by custom id before resubmitting anything.
  • Polling and retrieval. Poll batches with backoff; when a batch ends, download results promptly (well inside the retention period) into raw object storage, keyed by batch id, then parse. Results are matched by custom id, never by position.
  • Validation and outcomes. Succeeded responses are validated against the output schema (structured output via a JSON schema or a tool definition); invalid output is a failure class of its own. Errored requests are classified as retryable (overload, rate limit) or not (invalid request); expired and canceled requests are re-queued; invalid outputs are retried at most once with the same prompt, then routed to a review queue, because repeating a deterministic failure only costs money.
  • Writes. The enriched table is a MERGE keyed by doc_id with a version guard: apply only if the result's content_hash equals the document's current hash (or the result is newer by change sequence). A stale result is stored in history but never overwrites the current row. Every row carries prompt_version, model_snapshot, schema_version, batch_id, custom_id and enriched_at.
  • Backfills. A prompt or model change creates a new (prompt_version, model_snapshot) target; a backfill queue enumerates documents lazily and feeds the same scheduler at a lower priority with its own daily budget. Readers see one consistent version per row; a target_version view shows backfill progress, and consumers that need homogeneity can filter on the version.
  • Privacy and observability. Logs carry ids, hashes and counts, never document text. Metrics: queue age, units per state, batch durations, outcome mix per batch, validation failure rate by prompt version, cost per day from usage fields.

Competing designs to accept. Workflow engines (Airflow, Dagster, Temporal) owning the state machine; a stream processor feeding a queue of work units; storing state in the lakehouse instead of an OLTP table if updates are transactional; synchronous calls for a small urgent slice (with a clear reason). A candidate who keys work by doc_id only must explain how a stale result is prevented from overwriting a newer one.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Duplicate submission after a crash; results discarded because they were matched by position; the result retention period passing before download; a backfill consuming the organization's limits; schema drift in model output; very long documents exceeding the context window (chunk or skip with a flag); hot customers whose imports dwarf the daily change rate; cost overruns from retrying deterministic failures.

Incident guidance.

  • Backfill throttles interactive products: pause the backfill queue immediately (it is a separate queue for this reason), confirm interactive error rates recover, then resume with a lower per-pipeline budget derived from the limits headroom; add an alert on the organization's limit utilisation and make backfills yield automatically above a threshold.
  • 30% expired on a heavy day: the work units are still queued for retry, so nothing is lost; resubmit expired units first (they are the oldest), split into smaller batches, and check whether the volume (daily change plus the import) simply exceeded what the processing window absorbs; for imports, admit them through the backfill queue rather than the daily one so they cannot cause the daily deadline to slip.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Units were recorded as queued before submission and the batch id is recorded on return; on restart, list recent batches, map their custom ids back to units, and only resubmit units with no batch. (2) Both results are stored; only the one whose content_hash matches the current document is applied, so arrival order does not matter. (3) Lower-priority queue, a budget per day, oldest or most-read documents first; the table shows mixed versions with explicit columns, and dashboards can filter. (4) Group failures by prompt version, model snapshot, document type and length; one prompt version failing across types is a prompt problem; failures concentrated in long or unusual documents are data problems; retry only the retryable classes. (5) Daily units ≈ documents × change rate; tokens per unit × batch price; the largest levers are change detection (hashing avoids no-op work), prompt length (and caching of a shared prefix where the batch interface supports it), and how often prompt changes trigger full backfills.

Rubric anchors. 2: re-enriches everything nightly or keys only by document; retries blindly; no version guard. 3: hash-based change detection, deterministic ids, idempotent merge with a version guard, outcome classes, separate backfill. 4: also crash-safe submission reconciliation, limits headroom for other users, validation-aware retry policy, cost estimate and lineage that makes any field traceable to its prompt and model.

Strong signals. Asks what happens to results that come back after the document changed; designs the custom id deliberately. Red flags. Matching results by position; logging prompts and outputs with document text for debugging.

ANT-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Ingest. A scheduled job pulls usage and cost reports at the finest grain needed (hour or day × workspace × API key × model × token type × processing mode) with a lookback equal to the revision window plus a margin. Each pulled bucket replaces the stored bucket (MERGE or partition overwrite keyed by the report grain), so revisions update rather than duplicate. Raw responses are kept with the pull time, which allows "as reported at" questions and audits. Pulls are paginated and rate-limit aware; a run is idempotent and can be re-run for any range.
  • Facts. fct_usage_hourly(hour, workspace_id, api_key_id, model, token_type, processing_mode, tokens, reported_cost, pulled_at). Token types: uncached input, cache write, cache read, output; processing mode: standard or batch. Additive measures only; rates are computed in the semantic layer.
  • Cost. Prefer the provider's reported cost per bucket where available, because it already applies the right price for token type and mode; keep a versioned price table (effective-dated by model, token type and mode) to compute an expected cost as a check and to estimate savings from caching and batch. The difference between computed and reported cost is a monitored metric, not a silent fix.
  • Ownership. dim_key_owner and dim_workspace_owner as SCD type 2 (valid_from, valid_to) from the registry, plus allocation rules for shared keys (tag-based shares, fixed percentages) with their own validity. The join uses the owner valid at the usage hour, so a mid-month reorganisation moves only later days. Unknown owners map to an explicit UNALLOCATED unit with an alert and an owner-assignment workflow.
  • Allocation. Split shared-key cost by the rule's weights with largest-remainder rounding so parts add exactly to the cent amount of each bucket (or of each month line, decided once and documented).
  • Month close. Provisional close a few days after month end from the facts; final close when the invoice arrives: compare totals, book the difference to an INVOICE_ADJUSTMENT line allocated pro rata (or to a central cost centre), freeze the month (snapshot tables keyed by close version). Revisions after close create adjustment lines in the next open month; the closed snapshot is never rewritten.
  • Access and serving. Row-level security by business unit on the detail; finance sees all; daily dashboards read the open month and show "provisional" until close. Key ids are shown but no request content ever enters this pipeline.
  • Quality checks. Freshness per pull, completeness per hour (no missing buckets), totals per day stable outside the revision window, unallocated share below a threshold, computed vs reported cost within a tolerance.

Competing designs to accept. Taking only daily data if hourly is not needed; snapshotting the whole report every run and selecting the latest per bucket (simple and auditable, more storage); allocating by workspace rather than key when keys move between workspaces, provided the choice is stated; computing cost entirely from a price table if reconciled to the invoice with an explicit adjustment.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Append-only ingestion double counting revised buckets; joining to the current owner and rewriting history; rounding that leaves cents unassigned; silently re-opening closed months; price tables that drift from the provider's; rate-limited pulls that fall behind and leave gaps; very high key cardinality at the largest scale (aggregate early to the grain finance needs).

Follow-up guidance. (1) The closed month stays as sent; the correction becomes an adjustment line in the current month with a reference to the original period, visible to the affected units. (2) Compare by day, model, token type and mode to localise it: a missing token type (often cache writes or batch), a price change mid-month, hours outside the pull window, currency or rounding; book any unexplained remainder to the adjustment line and track it. (3) Attribute by the key's owner at usage time if keys are the unit of accountability, or by workspace if budgets and limits are managed per workspace; either way, the history table makes the move explicit. (4) Applications must send their own end-customer identifier (for example as request metadata or by using separate keys or workspaces per tenant); never infer customers from prompt content, and keep end-customer identifiers pseudonymous in this pipeline.

Rubric anchors. 2: nightly append of reports, current-owner joins, no reconciliation. 3: idempotent overlap pulls at the report grain, SCD ownership joined at usage time, explicit unallocated bucket, reconciliation with the invoice. 4: also a two-step close with frozen snapshots and adjustment lines, exact rounding, versioned prices used as a check, and clear access control.

Strong signals. Asks how late revisions arrive before designing the pull; insists the month total equals the invoice exactly. Red flags. "Re-pull everything each night and overwrite" without considering closed months; allocating unowned cost proportionally and hiding it.

ANT-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Telemetry event contract (stream_id, seq, event_type, block_index NULL, block_type NULL, emitted_at, host_id, schema_version, payload_bytes, delta_tokens NULL, stop_reason NULL, usage_output_tokens NULL, error_type NULL). (stream_id, seq) is the identity: duplicates collapse on it and order is by seq, never by timestamp. A delta record stores its size and token count, never the text. Pings are counted, not stored individually.
  • Request/stream context written once at acceptance: (stream_id, request_id, workspace_id, api_key_id, model, accepted_at, dequeued_at, first_byte_at, region). Queueing time = dequeued_at − accepted_at stays its own column so a scheduling change cannot masquerade as a model change.
  • fct_stream (one row per stream, always): accepted_at, first_event_at, first_delta_at (any block), first_text_delta_at, last_delta_at, ended_at, end_state completed | error | client_disconnect | timeout_closed, stop_reason, error_type, output_tokens (from the final usage), delta_count, max_gap_ms, block_count by type, sampled flag. Derived: TTFT_any = first_delta_at − accepted_at, TTFT_visible = first_text_delta_at − accepted_at (NULL when no text), time to last token, output tokens per second = output_tokens / (last_delta_at − first_delta_at) (NULL when fewer than two deltas or zero tokens).
  • fct_stream_block (one row per content block): stream_id, block_index, block_type text | tool_use | thinking | …, started_at, first_delta_at, stopped_at, delta_count, bytes, tokens. Answers "how long does thinking delay visible text" and tool-call timing without event data.
  • Event grain: kept only for streams sampled by hash(stream_id) mod N, all events of the stream, for {{raw_retention}}; used for debugging and to validate the summariser, not for dashboards.
  • Assembly: a stateful stream processor keyed by stream_id buffers events, dedups on seq, and closes the stream on message stop, on an error event, or on an inactivity timeout (e.g. 2–5 minutes after the last event, or a host-death signal); the timeout path writes end_state = timeout_closed with what is known. Late events after close produce a corrected row (upsert by stream_id, version column) rather than a second row.
  • Percentiles: per (model, workspace, hour) store a mergeable histogram or sketch (fixed log buckets, t-digest, KLL/DDSketch) of each latency; daily and fleet-wide percentiles come from merging sketches, never from averaging percentiles.

Competing designs to accept. Computing the stream summary in the serving tier and emitting one record per stream (plus sampled events), if the candidate handles host death (no summary emitted) with a server-side registry of open streams or a reaper. A lakehouse table of events partitioned by hour with a batch summariser, if they meet the 15-minute target with micro-batches and still close incomplete streams. Exact percentiles from the stream fact (it is one row per stream and affordable) instead of sketches, at Medium.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Event volume ({{daily_streams}} × {{events_per_stream}}); hot streams with thousands of deltas; streams that never close; duplicates and reordering from retries; timestamp ties; per-host clock skew (all timings for one stream come from one host, which helps); averaging percentiles; event-level sampling biasing gaps; text leaking into telemetry through error messages.

Incident guidance.

  • Message start moved earlier, TTFT "improved" 40%: the metric measured to the first event of any type, which is not a token. Redefine TTFT to the first delta (any) and first text delta, keep time to first event as a separate infrastructure metric, backfill from fct_stream for the period, annotate the dashboard. Guardrail: a contract test that the first-token metric ignores non-content events, and an alert when two TTFT variants diverge suddenly.
  • 2% of streams missing, mostly errors: summary only on message stop. Close on error events and on inactivity timeout too; backfill from the sampled events where possible and from request logs for counts; publish a corrected error rate. Guardrail: reconcile stream count in fct_stream with accepted requests per hour; alert on any gap.
  • Event-level sampling inflated gaps: sampling decided per record means consecutive sampled events are far apart. Switch to stream-level sampling by hash; compute max_gap only from complete streams (or in the summariser, which sees all events before sampling); mute the stall alert until the fix lands and recompute its baseline.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Name both variants; thinking-first stream: TTFT_any is the thinking delta, TTFT_visible is later; zero output tokens: TTFT NULL, counted in a separate "no output" share, never as 0. (2) Inactivity timeout or host-death signal in the stream processor; end_state and partial counts recorded. (3) Percentiles are not linear; store sketches or histograms and merge them. (4) The alert reads fct_stream (max_gap_ms) for closed streams, or a per-stream rolling state in the processor for in-flight stalls; latency = summariser lag. (5) Versioned contract with additive fields; block_type is open-ended text with a mapped "other"; dashboards read named columns that keep their meaning.

Rubric anchors. 2: one events table queried directly for everything, or TTFT defined vaguely. 3: stream and block facts with precise TTFT variants, stream-level sampling, incomplete streams represented. 4: also order-tolerant assembly with versions, mergeable percentile storage, a versioned contract, and incident answers that name the broken definition.

Strong signals. Asks "first token of what?" before drawing tables; keeps queueing separate; samples by stream unprompted. Red flags. Storing delta text; ordering by timestamp; averaging p95s; summary rows only for completed streams.

ANT-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • fct_request (request_id, workspace_id, api_key_id, model, received_at, end_user_ref NULL, stop_reason, n_tool_definitions, n_tool_use_blocks_new, n_tool_result_blocks_new, input/output tokens).
  • dim_tool_version (tool_key, workspace_id, name, schema_fingerprint, first_seen_at, last_seen_at) where tool_key = hash(workspace_id, name, schema_fingerprint). A schema change under the same name is a new version of the same named tool; trend charts can group by name with a version marker.
  • fct_tool_call (one row per tool_use id, the central fact): tool_use_id, workspace_id, tool_key, emitted_in_request_id, emitted_at, parallel_group_size, position_in_response, input_bytes, input_schema_valid, result_first_seen_request_id NULL, result_first_seen_at NULL, result_is_error NULL, result_bytes NULL, status open|answered|unanswered|dropped_from_history, run_id.
  • Linking: when a request arrives, parse its tool_result blocks; for each tool_use_id not yet answered, set the result columns (first seen wins); ids already answered are history and are ignored. Tool-use blocks in the request's history whose ids are already known are ignored; new tool_use ids appear only in responses. Matching is always by id, never by position or order.
  • Agent run: a chain of requests linked because request N+1 answers a tool_use emitted in response N (run_id = id of the first request in the chain; a union-find over "answers a call from" edges). Optionally refined with end_user_ref. A run ends when a response stops for a reason other than tool use, or when no follow-up arrives within a timeout. Stated limitation: two chains merged or split by edited history are possible; runs without tool use are single requests.
  • Unanswered: status becomes unanswered when no result has been seen within a timeout (e.g. 1 hour) of emission; dropped_from_history when a later request in the same run no longer contains the tool_use block and no result (a framework summarised it away).
  • Round-trip time: result_first_seen_at − emitted_at, named "client round trip" (tool execution + developer processing + network + queueing), never "tool latency".
  • Privacy: inputs and results are never stored; schema validity is computed in flight; sizes and error flags only.

Competing designs to accept. A run defined by a client-supplied end-user id plus a time gap, if the candidate says how many requests lack the id and what the metric means then. A prefix-hash approach to recognise history, if they handle edited history by falling back to id-based linking. Graph storage of request edges for run reconstruction.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Resent history double counting; position-based pairing with parallel calls; retries with identical bodies; edited or summarised history; tool name collisions across workspaces; schema changes under the same name; timeouts that decide "unanswered" too early for slow tools; storing customer content in telemetry.

Incident guidance.

  • Retried identical requests, answered > calls: the pipeline counted each sighting of a result as an answer. Make answering idempotent per tool_use_id (first seen wins); dedup requests by body fingerprint within a short window for request counts; recompute affected days. Guardrail: invariant check answered ≤ emitted per workspace per day.
  • Unanswered jumps to 28% after history summarisation: the calls were answered before the history was summarised, or the summary dropped unanswered blocks. Distinguish dropped_from_history from unanswered, re-derive status from first-seen results, and tell the affected developers what the metric now means. Guardrail: alert on a step change per framework/user agent, not just per workspace.
  • Results paired by position with {{max_parallel}} parallel calls: rebuild the pairing by tool_use_id from the retained identifiers; restate the two tools' error rates. Guardrail: a contract test with shuffled result order.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Union-find chain over "answers a call from"; breaks with edited history and with parallel sub-agents. (2) Each call has its own row; partially answered groups leave some open until the timeout. (3) First-seen semantics by id; result time = first request that carried it. (4) Version by schema fingerprint; compare error rates per version and mark the change on the chart. (5) Success needs ground truth the API never sees (the developer's own outcome); report proxies honestly: runs ending with end_turn, runs abandoned mid-tool, error-flag rates; offer an opt-in outcome callback as a product idea.

Rubric anchors. 2: counts tool_use blocks per request (double counting history) or pairs by position. 3: tool call fact keyed by id, results linked by id with first-seen semantics, tool identity including schema. 4: also a defensible run definition with stated limits, unanswered vs dropped, honest round-trip naming, and privacy-preserving columns.

Strong signals. Notices immediately that statelessness means history is resent; keys everything on tool_use_id. Red flags. Storing tool inputs "for debugging"; inventing a conversation id the API does not provide; calling the round trip "tool latency".

ANT-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • dim_organization (org_id, name, plan, contract_start, merged_into_org_id NULL, merged_at NULL).
  • dim_member (member_key surrogate, org_id, idp_user_id NULL, created_at, deprovisioned_at NULL, attributes_purged_at NULL). One member_key per person per organization; a returning person is matched by idp_user_id first, then by a verified email match within a policy window, and reactivated rather than recreated (or linked with previous_member_key when the policy says it is a new engagement). Email lives in the attribute history, never as the key.
  • member_attributes_scd2 (member_key, valid_from, valid_to, department, manager_member_key, cost_centre, employment_status, email, display_name, source_sync_id, recorded_at). A sync produces a new version only when attributes actually change; effective date is the identity provider's when supplied, otherwise the sync time; a late change with an earlier effective date splits the open interval and the days in between are listed for restatement. Each sync batch is validated (e.g. reject or quarantine a batch where > 5% of members lose a department) before it touches history.
  • seat_assignment (member_key, seat_type, assigned_at, unassigned_at NULL, assigned_by manual|sync|trial) as intervals; no overlapping intervals per member and seat type (exclusion constraint or check in the loader).
  • fct_member_activity_daily (org_id, member_key, activity_date (org's time zone), surface web|desktop|mobile, messages_sent, sessions, first_at, last_at). No content.
  • Derived: weekly/monthly active members by distinct member_key over days (stored per period, or as per-member activity bitmaps so periods can be combined exactly); utilisation = active members ÷ assigned seats on the period's last day (or average), stated; activity of members without a seat on that day reported separately.
  • Billing: at quarter close, compute the peak from the interval table exactly (sweep over assignment start/end events per organization) or from daily maximum concurrent seats, and write billing_peak (org_id, quarter, peak_seats, method, computed_at, input_hash), immutable; corrections are new rows with reason and approval.
  • Purge: after the purge period, null the personal columns in all attribute versions (email, display_name, manager) and set attributes_purged_at; member_key, department and counts remain, so reports stay additive.
  • Merger: the acquired org gets merged_into_org_id and merged_at; members are mapped to the surviving org with a member_merge_map (old_member_key, new_member_key) so people with seats in both become one; reports after the merge read the surviving org; the quarter's peak is computed over the union of seat intervals after mapping, not by adding peaks.

Competing designs to accept. Daily periodic snapshot of seats and attributes (simple, robust) instead of intervals, if the candidate states what intra-day changes it misses and whether the contract cares. Type-1 department with a separate department-history table only for reports. Current-department attribution, if the candidate presents it as an explicit admin choice and offers both views.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Email as key; current-department joins rewriting history; bad sync batches; late effective dates; overlapping seat intervals; summing weekly actives; peaks summed across merged orgs; purge breaking joins; time zones for "day"; trials and post-removal activity.

Incident guidance.

  • Empty department for 30% of members: a sync batch should never be applied blindly. Quarantine batches that change an unusual share of members; for this one, close the bad versions by reverting to the prior values (new versions effective from the original start, with the bad interval marked invalid), rerun the affected week's report, and tell the admin. Guardrail: batch-level anomaly checks and a "pending sync" state.
  • Returning contractors got new ids: merge each new member_key into the previous one through the identity rule (idp_user_id or verified email), fix seat intervals so they do not overlap, restate cohort reports, and credit the double-counted seat day in billing. Guardrail: match on idp_user_id before creating a member; alert on bulk creations matching deprovisioned emails.
  • Merged organizations' peaks added: recompute the peak over the union of mapped intervals; people in both count once; document the method in billing_peak and issue a correction row.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Active = at least one message sent that day (org time zone); weekly active = distinct members active on any day of the week; utilisation stated with numerator and denominator; seatless activity shown as its own line. (2) The open version is split at Monday; Monday to Thursday activity rows now join to the new department; the restatement list is exactly those member-days. (3) Interval sweep or daily max over seat_assignment, frozen into billing_peak at close. (4) Before: full attributes; after: same rows with personal columns null and purged_at set. (5) merged_into, member map, union of intervals.

Rubric anchors. 2: one users table keyed by email with a current department column. 3: surrogate member key, type-2 attributes, seat intervals, daily activity fact, as-of-date attribution. 4: also late-change restatement, batch validation, an immutable billing artefact, a purge that preserves counts, and a merge model.

Strong signals. Asks what identifies a person before drawing tables; separates billing artefacts from live tables. Red flags. Email as primary key; adding weekly actives; updating department in place; summing peaks.

ANT-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • dim_model_snapshot (snapshot_id, model_family, released_at, deprecated_at NULL, retires_at NULL, announced_at); lifecycle dates from public announcements.
  • model_alias_history (alias, snapshot_id, announced_from NULL, observed_from, observed_to NULL): derived from fct_request (first and last response where requested_model = alias was served by the snapshot); announcement kept separately. It is a type-2 dimension whose validity comes from observation.
  • fct_request (request_id, app_id, api_key_id, workspace_id, template_id, template_version, requested_model, served_snapshot, experiment_id NULL, arm NULL, task_type, sent_at, ttft_ms, total_ms, input_tokens, output_tokens, stop_reason, status, cost_computed_at_price_version).
  • fct_feedback (request_id, rating, rated_at) and fct_eval_score (request_id, grader_id, grader_version, score, scored_at): late-arriving facts keyed by request; reports for the last 7 days are labelled provisional.
  • experiment_assignment (experiment_id, unit_type end_user|session, unit_id, arm, assigned_at) and experiment_arm (experiment_id, arm, requested_model, template_version): analysis by assignment (intention to treat), not by what served.
  • Comparison queries: group by served_snapshot within strata (app, template_version, task_type); report per-stratum differences and a weighted average over a common mix; show counts and intervals; latency compared as TTFT and tokens per second as well as total time, since output length differs.
  • Retirement report: from fct_request over the last N days: distinct app_id, api_key_id, template_id where served_snapshot = X, split into "pinned" (requested_model = X) and "via alias" (requested_model ≠ X).

Competing designs to accept. A single "model" column that stores the served snapshot plus a separate requested_model only in raw logs, if the candidate shows the alias questions are still answerable. Bayesian or bootstrap intervals instead of frequentist ones. A difference-in-differences between applications that switched and those that did not, if they state the assumption.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Grouping by requested name; template changes confounded with model changes; mix shift across task types; feedback selection bias and low rates; output-length differences inflating total latency; late feedback making recent days look different; retirement lists built from configuration instead of traffic.

Incident guidance.

  • Alias moved, "same model" step change: the dashboard grouped by requested name. Add served_snapshot as the default grouping, annotate alias moves from the observed history, and send the application team the per-snapshot view. Guardrail: an alert when the distribution of served_snapshot for a requested name changes.
  • Template and snapshot changed the same day: unidentifiable from that application's traffic alone. Options: roll one change back for a randomised slice, use other applications' switch (same template not changed) as a comparison, or run the offline evaluation on old/new template × old/new snapshot. Say plainly what cannot be concluded.
  • Retirement report missed alias users: rebuild it from served_snapshot in traffic, not from configuration; include keys and templates; re-send 60 days ahead and track each owner to zero traffic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Per served snapshot for model owners; per requested name for application owners who care about their experience; both from the same fact. (2) Stratify by task_type and show mix per snapshot; weighted comparison. (3) The served-snapshot query split pinned/via-alias. (4) Assignment by end user, analysis by assigned arm including failures and retries; retries are outcomes, not exclusions. (5) Minimum counts per cell, intervals, and a "not enough data" state.

Rubric anchors. 2: one model column, mean metrics, no template version. 3: requested vs served, snapshot dimension with lifecycle dates, template version, late-arriving feedback. 4: also stratified or randomised comparisons with stated confounding and bias, observation-based alias history, and a traffic-based retirement report.

Strong signals. Separates requested from served in the first minute; raises confounding with template changes. Red flags. "Compare the averages before and after"; treating thumbs-down rate as unbiased quality; alias history typed by hand.

ANT-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL; {{window_start}}, {{window_end}}, {{report_at}}, {{min_users}} and {{min_orgs}} are the instance's values. At Medium the organization threshold is 1, and at Medium and Hard every facet row was classified before the report time, so the same query applies at every level.)

WITH facet AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (conversation_id) conversation_id, task_category
  FROM conversation_facets
  WHERE classified_at <= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{report_at}}'
  ORDER BY conversation_id, classified_at DESC
), counted AS (
  SELECT c.conversation_id, c.user_key, c.org_id, f.task_category,
         date_trunc('week', c.created_at)::date AS week_start
  FROM conversations c
  JOIN orgs o  ON o.org_id = c.org_id AND NOT o.analytics_opt_out
  JOIN facet f ON f.conversation_id = c.conversation_id
  WHERE c.created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{window_start}}'
    AND c.created_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '{{window_end}}'
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM deletion_requests d WHERE d.conversation_id = c.conversation_id)
), cells AS (
  SELECT week_start, task_category,
         COUNT(*)                AS conversations,
         COUNT(DISTINCT user_key) AS users,
         COUNT(DISTINCT org_id)   AS orgs
  FROM counted
  GROUP BY week_start, task_category
), verdict AS (
  SELECT cells.*, (users >= {{min_users}} AND orgs >= {{min_orgs}}) AS publishable
  FROM cells
), other AS (
  SELECT k.week_start, 'other' AS task_category,
         COUNT(*)                  AS conversations,
         COUNT(DISTINCT k.user_key) AS users,
         COUNT(DISTINCT k.org_id)   AS orgs
  FROM counted k
  JOIN verdict v ON v.week_start = k.week_start AND v.task_category = k.task_category
  WHERE NOT v.publishable
  GROUP BY k.week_start
)
SELECT week_start, task_category, conversations, users, orgs FROM verdict WHERE publishable
UNION ALL
SELECT week_start, task_category, conversations, users, orgs FROM other
WHERE users >= {{min_users}} AND orgs >= {{min_orgs}}
ORDER BY week_start, task_category;

Explanation. Every rule about a single conversation (window, opt-out, deletion, category, week) is settled once in counted, one row per conversation, so nothing downstream can double count. DISTINCT ON keeps one facet row per conversation, the latest known at the report time; filtering facets by report_at makes the report reproducible, while deletions are honoured whatever their time because reproducibility never brings deleted data back. Cells are aggregated with distinct users and organizations, judged against inclusive thresholds, and the conversations of the failed cells are re-aggregated from the rows, so a user who appears in two suppressed categories counts once in other. other is itself an aggregate and is published only if it clears the thresholds.

Complexity. One sort or hash for DISTINCT ON over the facets, one hash aggregate over counted conversations, and a second aggregate over the suppressed subset: linear in the window's conversations plus sorts. At production scale this is computed per week incrementally: keep per-(week, category) sets of user and org keys (or exact distinct counts recomputed only for weeks touched by deletions or re-classification), never approximate sketches for a privacy threshold.

Dialect notes. DISTINCT ON is PostgreSQL only: Snowflake and BigQuery use QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY conversation_id ORDER BY classified_at DESC) = 1, Spark SQL and MySQL 8 a subquery with ROW_NUMBER(). Week start: date_trunc('week', ts) is Monday-based in PostgreSQL and Snowflake by default (Snowflake's WEEK_START parameter can change it); BigQuery needs DATE_TRUNC(DATE(ts), WEEK(MONDAY)) or ISOWEEK because WEEK starts on Sunday; Spark's date_trunc('week', ts) is Monday-based; MySQL needs DATE_SUB(DATE(ts), INTERVAL WEEKDAY(ts) DAY). Timestamp literals: '…'::TIMESTAMP_TZ (Snowflake), TIMESTAMP '…' (BigQuery, UTC). None of these variants is executed here.

Edge cases built into the data. A cell at exactly min_users (published); cells one user short; two suppressed cells in the same week that share a user (so summing their users overstates other); a week whose only suppressed cell is too small for other to be published; a cell lifted to the threshold only by a user whose conversations are all deleted; a cell lifted only by users of the opted-out organization; unclassified conversations; a conversation exactly at the window start (included) and exactly at its end (excluded); a conversation exactly at Monday 00:00 inside the window; conversations before and after the window. Hard adds re-classified conversations (latest facet wins) and a cell with enough users from too few organizations. Very Hard adds a retention window that starts and ends mid-week (partial weeks), a conversation first classified after the report time (unclassified for this report), a re-classification after the report time (ignored), and a deletion requested after the report time (still honoured).

Common mistakes. Counting deleted or opted-out conversations; > instead of >=; summing users across suppressed cells; dropping suppressed cells instead of merging them; publishing other unconditionally; LEFT JOIN to facets that lets unclassified conversations into other; Sunday-based weeks; ignoring the window or retention cut-off; ignoring the organization threshold; using the first facet, or every facet row; using facets classified after the report time; honouring only deletions requested before the report. Each has a diagnostic.

Follow-up guidance. (1) With a published weekly total, total minus published cells equals other (or the single suppressed cell, if other is withheld and only one cell was suppressed): complementary suppression or not publishing totals; across reports, overlapping windows allow differencing too. (2) Store per-(week, category) distinct key sets or recompute only touched weeks; republish with a revision note; if a published cell falls below the threshold, it moves into other. (3) Yes: two adjacent reports can differ by one user; mitigations are rounding to a base, small calibrated noise (differential privacy) or stable cell membership rules; say what the threshold does and does not guarantee. (4) Keep the published aggregates (which passed the threshold) and their run metadata, not the raw rows; a reproduction request gets the published numbers and an explanation that the inputs were deleted by policy.

Rubric anchors. 2: right shape but counts deleted/opted-out conversations or sums users into other. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also explains differencing risk, incremental recomputation after deletions, and why facets are cut at the report time while deletions are not.

Strong signals. Asks whether other must itself meet the threshold; mentions that sketches are not acceptable for a privacy threshold near its boundary. Red flags. SUM(users) for other; treating a deletion as optional for reproducibility; publishing a total next to suppressed cells without noticing the leak.
ANT-L3-05.reference_sql:
WITH facet AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (conversation_id) conversation_id, task_category
  FROM conversation_facets
  WHERE classified_at <= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{report_at}}'
  ORDER BY conversation_id, classified_at DESC
), counted AS (
  SELECT c.conversation_id, c.user_key, c.org_id, f.task_category,
         date_trunc('week', c.created_at)::date AS week_start
  FROM conversations c
  JOIN orgs o  ON o.org_id = c.org_id AND NOT o.analytics_opt_out
  JOIN facet f ON f.conversation_id = c.conversation_id
  WHERE c.created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{window_start}}'
    AND c.created_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '{{window_end}}'
    AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM deletion_requests d WHERE d.conversation_id = c.conversation_id)
), cells AS (
  SELECT week_start, task_category,
         COUNT(*)                AS conversations,
         COUNT(DISTINCT user_key) AS users,
         COUNT(DISTINCT org_id)   AS orgs
  FROM counted
  GROUP BY week_start, task_category
), verdict AS (
  SELECT cells.*, (users >= {{min_users}} AND orgs >= {{min_orgs}}) AS publishable
  FROM cells
), other AS (
  SELECT k.week_start, 'other' AS task_category,
         COUNT(*)                  AS conversations,
         COUNT(DISTINCT k.user_key) AS users,
         COUNT(DISTINCT k.org_id)   AS orgs
  FROM counted k
  JOIN verdict v ON v.week_start = k.week_start AND v.task_category = k.task_category
  WHERE NOT v.publishable
  GROUP BY k.week_start
)
SELECT week_start, task_category, conversations, users, orgs FROM verdict WHERE publishable
UNION ALL
SELECT week_start, task_category, conversations, users, orgs FROM other
WHERE users >= {{min_users}} AND orgs >= {{min_orgs}}
ORDER BY week_start, task_category;

ANT-L4-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Edge summariser at the gateway. The handler that owns the client connection runs a small per-stream state machine and, using the host's monotonic clock, records: request received; message_start flushed; first content_block_delta flushed (first content, split by block type: text, thinking, tool input); each content event's flush time folded into running statistics (count, bytes, maximum gap, number of gaps above the stall threshold, total stalled time; pings excluded from progress); how the stream ended (message_stop, error event with its type, server close, client close) and which side closed first; stop reason and output tokens from message_delta; model, region, organisation, workspace, API key id, request id, SDK user agent. On close it emits one compact summary record. Per-event timelines are kept only for a small sample (plus every stream that stalled or ended abnormally) for 7 days.
  • Server-side record. The inference server emits its own summary keyed by request id: queue wait, prefill time, first token produced, tokens generated, server-side completion or error. Comparing "first token produced" with "first content flushed" isolates the gateway and network-buffering segment.
  • Join and aggregation. Both streams of records go to a regional log keyed by request id. A stream job joins them with a bounded wait (for example a few minutes; streams can run long, so the gateway summary is emitted at close and the join waits for the later of the two), and emits a joined record; unmatched records after the bound are emitted alone and counted. Durations are computed within one host's monotonic clock (gateway durations from gateway timestamps, server durations from server timestamps), never by subtracting timestamps from different hosts. Aggregates per (model, region, organisation, minute) carry counts by end type, stall counts and mergeable latency sketches (time to first content, maximum gap) so regions and minutes merge without averaging percentiles.
  • Serving. A real-time OLAP store for on-call (per model and region, {{freshness}} freshness) and an organisation-scoped view for enterprise admins with row-level security on organisation id; per-key and per-workspace breakdowns only inside the organisation. Summaries kept 90 days in columnar storage; sampled per-event detail 7 days.
  • Privacy. The schema has no content fields; the summariser counts bytes and events but never copies payloads. A contract test fails the build on any new field not on the allow-list.
  • Client side (optional). An SDK can report sampled client-side timings (time to first rendered token, client-observed stalls) keyed by request id. These are opt-in, sampled, treated as untrusted (clamped, outlier-filtered) and used to validate the gateway's view, not to replace it.

Competing designs to accept. Shipping every event to a stream processor and sessionising by request id with a gap window, if the candidate costs it (events per day = streams × deltas per stream) and handles the window end; doing the join in batch with a separate real-time path for on-call; eBPF or proxy-level socket timing instead of handler instrumentation. Any design that measures at the client-facing hop and defines stalls precisely is acceptable.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Event volume if every delta is shipped; clock skew when durations cross hosts; long streams that outlive a session window; buffering between the generator and the socket hiding stalls or delays; overload errors mid-stream that client retries amplify; high-cardinality labels (per key) on the operational metrics path; mistaking client disconnects for server failures.

Incident guidance.

  • Idle timeout below the ping interval: the gateway sees server-side close by the load balancer, or the client sees a reset with no error event; end-type counts show a rise in "closed without message_stop and without error" concentrated on long pre-first-delta waits. Recovery: restore the timeout above the ping interval with margin. Prevention: an alert on abnormal-end rate by end type, and a synthetic long-wait stream probe that runs through the real path.
  • Overload errors mid-stream: per-region error-event rate after first content, and request-id retry chains (same organisation, similar input size, seconds apart). Recovery: shed earlier (reject before streaming starts, where an overloaded response is cheap to retry), return retry-after guidance, ensure SDK retries use backoff with jitter. Prevention: alert on error-after-content rate; capacity headroom per region.
  • 64 KB flush buffer: "first content flushed" minus "first token produced" jumps while server metrics are flat; short answers are worst affected. Roll back; add the flush-delay segment as a first-class metric with an alert, and a canary that compares flush timing before and after gateway deploys.
  • Clock drift: negative cross-host durations are the symptom. Fix the design so durations use one host's monotonic clock; alert on host clock offset; quarantine records from drifting hosts rather than publishing false stalls.

Follow-up guidance. Push on the exact definition of a stall (gap between consecutive content events, pings excluded, threshold {{stall_threshold}}, measured at flush), on how a stream that outlives any window is finalised, and on how the candidate separates the client's departure from a server fault (who closed first, error event present or not, bytes the client acknowledged if available).

Rubric anchors. 2: reuses server-side TTFT and average latency, ships every event without costing it, no end-type classification. 3: gateway-side per-stream summaries, precise stall and end definitions, join by request id with bounded lateness, sketches for percentiles, no content in telemetry. 4: also single-clock durations, sampled per-event detail for abnormal streams, organisation-scoped views, optional client timings handled as untrusted, and crisp handling of every incident.

Strong signals. Asks which hop the customer actually sees; separates "first event" from "first content"; brings up retries amplifying overload. Red flags. Logging delta text for debugging; computing durations across hosts' wall clocks; averaging per-region p95 values.

ANT-L4-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Price catalogue. Rows of (model, token class, batch flag, price per million tokens in fixed-point minor units with stated precision, effective_from, effective_to, version). Changes are reviewed, validated by invariants (cache-read price below ordinary input below cache-write; batch price below interactive) and loaded ahead of their effective time. Each priced record stores the catalogue version it used.
  • Usage records. On completion, the serving layer emits one usage record per request id: organisation, workspace and key ids as of the request, model, batch flag, region, request time, the four token counts. Batch requests carry their completion time; per the stated policy they are attributed at completion.
  • Exact path (ledger). A stream job prices each record with the catalogue version in force at the request's attribution time and upserts into a ledger keyed by request id (insert-if-absent), so redelivery cannot double-count. Daily cost per (organisation, workspace, key, model, day) is an aggregation of the ledger; late records (a region's backlog) land in their correct day, and published days are corrected by adjustment rows, never edited silently. The invoice is built from the same ledger, so reports reconcile by construction; rounding happens once, at a stated grain (for example per line item on the invoice), with sub-unit precision kept upstream.
  • Fast path (enforcement). Each region keeps an in-memory counter per workspace fed by its own usage stream (priced with the same catalogue) and periodically synchronised from the ledger's authoritative month-to-date total. The global limit is split into regional allowances that rebalance every few seconds based on recent spend, so the request path only reads local state. Admission: if month-to-date spend plus the region's in-flight estimate is at or above the allowance, reject. For in-flight estimates, either reserve input cost plus a typical output estimate (not the maximum, which blocks too early) and release on completion, or accept a measured overshoot.
  • Overshoot bound. Worst case ≈ (concurrent in-flight requests at the moment of crossing × maximum cost per request) + (spend rate × detection delay up to {{enforce_within}}). State it and shrink it with per-workspace concurrency caps near the limit, smaller rebalance intervals, and stricter reservations above 95%.
  • Failure policy. If a region's counter store is unavailable: fail open for a bounded time with a conservative local cap derived from the last known headroom, and fail closed for workspaces already within a small margin of their limit. Alert, and record who absorbs any overshoot (policy decision with finance).
  • Admin view. Daily cost per key and workspace from the ledger (with an "as of" time and a marker for days still receiving late usage); a reconciliation report that lists, per invoice line, the request ids behind it.

Competing designs to accept. A central strongly consistent counter in one region with regional caching, if the candidate keeps synchronous cross-region calls off the request path; pricing at the edge versus in the stream job; a token-bucket-style allowance per region. Any design that separates the exact ledger from the approximate counter and states the overshoot bound is acceptable.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Double counting on redelivery; floating-point drift; price changes racing with lagging streams (price must follow request time, not processing time); key moves mis-attributed; counters drifting from the ledger after failover; hot workspaces concentrating counter updates; batch completions crossing month boundaries.

Incident guidance.

  • Swapped cache prices: detect with catalogue invariants (should have blocked the load) and with a ledger check on effective price per token class. Recovery: correct the catalogue, reprice affected ledger records by catalogue version and time range, issue adjustment rows and customer credits where customers were overcharged, and decide with finance on undercharges. Prevention: invariant checks and a two-person review on price loads, plus a canary that compares priced totals before and after a catalogue change.
  • 25-minute overspend: per-region consumer lag and "counter freshness" (time since last update per workspace) should alert. Recovery: restart or rebalance the consumer, resync counters from the ledger. Prevention: alert on counter staleness beyond {{enforce_within}}; fail closed for workspaces near their limit when the counter is stale; decide and communicate whether the overspend is credited.
  • Batch crossing the month: the stated policy (attributed at completion) explains it; the console should show batch cost by completion time and the batch id, and documentation should say so. If customers need it by creation month, offer a report view keyed by batch creation while keeping the invoice rule unchanged.
  • Key moves double-counted: attribution must use the key's workspace as of each request, from a key-to-workspace history table (valid_from, valid_to), not a current-state join. Recompute the day, publish corrections, add a test with a mid-day move.

Follow-up guidance. Ask the candidate to compute the overshoot bound with numbers; probe on which clock (request time vs processing time) chooses the price; check whether they know that an approximate counter needs a source of truth to resync from.

Rubric anchors. 2: one counter used for both enforcement and invoices, float costs, no idempotency. 3: ledger keyed by request id, versioned prices, regional counters with a stated overshoot, attribution as of request time. 4: also regional allowance rebalancing, explicit fail-open/closed policy by headroom, reconciliation to invoice lines, correction model for late data, and clear handling of every incident including customer remediation.

Strong signals. Separates enforcement from billing correctness unprompted; prices by request time; asks how batch usage is attributed. Red flags. Synchronous cross-region calls per request; recomputing invoices from counters; silently editing published days.

ANT-L4-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Scoring. Classifiers run asynchronously next to the request path (with only the most severe, low-latency checks inline if policy requires). Each emits a score record: request id, account ids (organisation, key or app user), category, classifier version, threshold version, score, flagged boolean, model version, time. Content is not in the score record. For flagged requests from organisations whose agreements allow it, the minimal flagged excerpt goes to an encrypted evidence store with a {{flag_retention}} expiry; for organisations whose agreements forbid storage, the content-retention rule is applied before anything is written (a check on the organisation flag at the writer, not a later cleanup).
  • Aggregation. A stream job maintains per (account, category) windowed statistics (counts of scored and flagged requests over hours and days, rate, a sequential test or exponentially weighted rate against the category's base rate) so persistence is judged on rate and on enough evidence, not on raw count. A second job looks for cross-account spikes: per category, flag rate across all traffic per few minutes, plus grouping by shared features that are not content (new accounts, shared payment or signup attributes where policy allows, similar request shapes, the same flagged pattern id from a classifier).
